headline: RBA widely tipped to hike rates to 4.6% tomorrow as the Iran conflict keeps oil elevated and global markets push higher.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft had a strong night last session, jumping 3.66% to $516.17 USD. The market continues to reward Microsoft's AI story — investors are increasingly betting the Azure cloud and Copilot AI products will drive earnings growth. A Simply Wall St analysis flagged whether MSFT is now fully priced, but for now sentiment is firmly bullish.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI pulled back 2.71% today to $16.86, its biggest single-day move in the portfolio this session. This ETF holds a basket of AI-related stocks globally, so it tends to swing with broader sentiment around AI and tech. No single catalyst today — this looks like normal volatility in a high-growth thematic ETF.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE slipped 1.06% to $93.96 today. Emerging markets have been under pressure as rising oil prices (driven by the Iran-Hormuz conflict) squeeze importing economies, and the prospect of a domestic RBA rate hike adds pressure on the Aussie dollar outlook. Nothing structurally broken here.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google edged up 0.61% last session to $341.08 USD. Cloud revenue hitting $20B is a headline milestone, though some analysts flagged that free cash flow (the actual money left over after the business runs) dipped. Overall the long-term cloud and AI story remains intact.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two dipped a modest 0.76% last session to $201.44 USD. Nothing dramatic — GTA 6 remains the big catalyst on the horizon and a new leak roundup circulated online, but no material news changed the investment case. The stock is still down significantly from the invested cost, but the GTA 6 release remains the long-term thesis.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS edged down just 0.24% today to $538.08 — essentially flat. This broad US market ETF mirrors the performance of the entire US sharemarket, so tiny daily moves are normal. The underlying US market (S&P 500) was actually up last session, so today's slight ASX-listed dip is largely a currency and timing effect.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG was dead flat today, down just 2 cents to $76.27. This diversified fund holds shares across Australian and international markets, so it tends to be steady. No news to report — just a quiet day.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara Minerals didn't move at all today, closing flat at $3.84. The lithium sector remains subdued — there's no fresh catalyst to drive the price either way right now. The stock is still well below the invested cost, reflecting the broader lithium price slump since 2023.

watch_today.title: RBA rate decision tomorrow — brace for a hike
watch_today.detail: The Reserve Bank is widely expected to lift the cash rate to 4.6% tomorrow — its highest since 2011. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has already flagged the Middle East war and oil price surge as key drivers. If you have a mortgage, this could cost hundreds of dollars more per year. For your portfolio, higher rates can pressure growth stocks and ETFs short-term, but your long-term holdings should ride it out.

watch_today.title: MSFT — hold, strong AI tailwind continuing
watch_today.detail: Microsoft jumped 3.66% last session to $516.17 USD, now showing a 16.5% gain on your invested cost. The AI/Azure story is very much intact. No reason to sell — this is exactly the kind of long-term compounder you want to sit on. If you have spare cash, any dip is worth considering as a top-up.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — hold through the volatility
watch_today.detail: GXAI dropped 2.71% today and is now 10.7% below your cost. AI thematic ETFs are volatile by nature — they rise and fall sharply with sentiment. The long-term case for AI investment hasn't changed. Sit tight and let the thesis play out. This is noise, not a structural problem.

watch_today.title: TTWO — hold, GTA 6 remains the long-term bet
watch_today.detail: Take-Two slipped 0.76% last session and is 13.2% below your cost. That's uncomfortable, but the investment thesis is entirely about GTA 6's release. Until that launch date is set and the game ships, the stock will drift. Nothing broke today — hold and be patient.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — hold, lithium waiting for a catalyst
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals was flat again today at $3.84, and is down 43% on your cost — the steepest loss in the portfolio. There's no fresh catalyst right now, and the lithium sector broadly remains depressed. The long-term case depends on EV demand picking up and lithium supply tightening. Selling now locks in the loss — hold and reassess as the macro picture develops.

watch_today.title: Oil spiking on Iran-Hormuz standoff — watch for flow-on inflation
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) rose 2.13% last session to $94.38 USD a barrel — a meaningful jump driven by the US-Iran conflict and uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz. Higher oil means higher petrol prices and upward pressure on inflation, which could give the RBA extra reason to keep rates elevated longer. Worth watching this week.

world.summary: The Iran conflict continues to dominate global headlines, with the Strait of Hormuz still a flashpoint. US midterm integrity concerns are emerging, gold had a sharp pullback, and a Fitch warning about AI-driven recession risk is making the rounds.

stories.title: Trump rejects Iran's Hormuz deal — conflict drags on
stories.why_it_matters: Iran reportedly offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which about 20% of the world's oil flows — in exchange for a ceasefire, but Trump rejected the proposal. Tehran has since ignored further diplomatic overtures, leaving the conflict unresolved. This keeps oil supply uncertainty elevated and is a key reason crude prices jumped to $94 a barrel. Higher oil prices feed into everything from petrol at the bowser to airline tickets to grocery delivery costs.

stories.title: BBC reports from Yemen front lines as war escalates
stories.why_it_matters: The war in Yemen is escalating, with BBC journalists reporting directly from the front line. Yemen sits at the southern entrance to the Red Sea — another critical shipping lane for global trade. Disruption there, combined with the Hormuz standoff, puts two major oil and shipping routes under threat simultaneously. That's a significant supply chain risk for global goods prices.

stories.title: Five arrested near UK air base used by US bombers in Iran war
stories.why_it_matters: Five people were arrested near a UK air base being used by US bombers in the Iran conflict. The incident highlights how the war is extending beyond the Middle East, with Western nations' domestic security now caught up in the fallout. It raises the stakes for NATO allies and adds to uncertainty about how far the conflict could spread.

stories.title: Trump allies could exploit midterm 'counting window' to disrupt results
stories.why_it_matters: Experts are warning that allies of Trump could use a legal 'counting window' — a gap in US electoral rules about when and how votes are certified — to challenge or delay midterm election results. This is raising fears about political instability in the US heading into the midterms. Markets tend to hate political uncertainty, especially in the world's largest economy, so this is worth monitoring over the coming weeks.

stories.title: Fitch warns AI-driven market correction could tip US into recession
stories.why_it_matters: Credit ratings agency Fitch has flagged a scenario where a sharp correction in AI-inflated stock prices could push the US economy into recession and drag global growth below 1% — a level not seen outside of major crises. The warning is relevant to your portfolio because several holdings (MSFT, GOOG, GXAI) are heavily tied to the AI theme. It doesn't mean sell, but it's a reminder that AI valuations are elevated and a correction is a real risk to watch.

markets.summary: Last night's US session was broadly positive — the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both gained around half a percent. Microsoft was the standout mover. Gold had a rough night, dropping over 3%, while oil jumped sharply. The ASX had a modest positive day, up 0.17%. The Aussie dollar held steady around 70 US cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Quiet positive day for the ASX. The market is largely treading water ahead of tomorrow's RBA rate decision.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: US stocks edged higher last session, led by tech. Microsoft's strong run was a big contributor.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: The tech-heavy NASDAQ gained last night, broadly in line with the S&P 500. AI and cloud names drove sentiment.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil jumped 2.13% on continued uncertainty around the Iran-Hormuz standoff. Higher oil means higher petrol prices and more inflation pressure.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold had a sharp pullback, dropping over 3%. This is unusual for gold, which typically rises in times of conflict. Could reflect profit-taking after a strong run or shifting investor appetite.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar was steady, sitting just above 70 US cents. Holding up reasonably well despite rate hike expectations.

politics.summary: All roads lead to tomorrow's RBA decision — the cash rate is expected to rise to 4.6%, its highest in 15 years. Treasurer Chalmers is pointing to the Middle East war and oil prices as the trigger, while also touting a better-than-expected budget position.

stories.title: RBA tipped to hike rates to 4.6% tomorrow — highest since 2011
stories.why_it_matters: Markets and economists are nearly unanimous that the RBA will lift the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% tomorrow — the highest level since 2011. The main drivers are sticky inflation, a 60-year surge in building activity pushing up construction costs, and rising oil prices from the Middle East conflict. For borrowers, SBS reports this could cost hundreds of dollars more per year on a typical mortgage.

stories.title: Chalmers blames Middle East war for likely rate rise
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers is framing tomorrow's expected rate hike as largely a consequence of the Iran war driving oil prices higher, rather than a domestic economic failure. He argues the government's budget position is actually stronger than forecast — Bloomberg reported the deficit is coming in smaller than expected. The political framing matters: Labor wants to avoid being blamed for cost-of-living pain heading into the next election cycle.

stories.title: Building surge firing up inflation — giving RBA another reason to hike
stories.why_it_matters: The AFR reports Australia is experiencing its biggest building construction surge in 60 years, which sounds positive but is actually adding fuel to inflation. More construction means more demand for materials, trades, and labour — pushing prices up. This gives the RBA additional justification to raise rates, beyond just the oil price shock.

stories.title: Recession fears explode as Aussies feel 'exposed'
stories.why_it_matters: Consumer sentiment is souring, with recession fears growing among everyday Australians. Higher interest rates squeeze household budgets — less spending means slower economic growth, which can tip into recession if it goes too far. Fitch's global warning about sub-1% global growth adds to that anxiety. For investors, a domestic recession would likely weigh on ASX stocks but could also eventually force the RBA to cut rates, which would benefit bond and diversified ETF holders like VDHG.

ai.summary: Bill Gates is dominating AI headlines with a stark warning about unregulated AI potentially causing catastrophic harm. Meanwhile, the big AI labs are reportedly exploring a joint safety testing body, and tech-savvy users are finding ways to run multiple AI models from one workspace.

stories.title: Bill Gates warns unchecked AI could 'cause a billion deaths'
stories.why_it_matters: Bill Gates has issued one of the starkest public warnings yet about artificial intelligence, saying that AI systems powerful enough to cause a billion deaths could emerge without proper regulation. He's specifically calling for strict guardrails before AI reaches certain capability thresholds. While the 'billion deaths' figure sounds extreme, Gates is pointing to scenarios like AI being used to design bioweapons or automate cyberattacks at scale. It adds significant weight to the growing global debate about AI safety laws.

stories.title: Anthropic, OpenAI and Google in talks over joint AI testing body
stories.why_it_matters: The three most powerful AI companies — Anthropic (makers of Claude), OpenAI (ChatGPT), and Google (Gemini) — are reportedly in discussions to create a shared body for testing AI systems before release. This would be a big deal: rather than each company marking its own homework, an independent testing group would assess whether AI models are safe to deploy. It's an early sign the industry may be moving toward self-regulation ahead of government-imposed rules.

stories.title: Former PM Gillard urges leaders to 'muscle up' on AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: Former Australian Prime Minister Julia Gillard is calling on world leaders to take stronger action on AI regulation, urging them to 'muscle up' rather than leaving tech companies to self-govern. Gillard is involved in global education and governance initiatives, and her comments reflect growing concern among political leaders that governments are moving too slowly relative to how fast AI is advancing.

stories.title: One dev ditched multiple AI subscriptions and built a single setup for Claude, GPT, Gemini & local models
stories.why_it_matters: A developer shared how they stopped paying for multiple separate AI subscriptions (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, local models) and built a single unified setup to access all of them from one interface. This is practical, money-saving advice for anyone using AI tools regularly — you can often avoid paying $20-30/month per tool by routing them through a single open-source hub. Handy if you're experimenting with different AI assistants.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is set — Roosters vs Knights at Accor Stadium on Sunday. Knights winger Phoenix Crossland learns his judiciary fate after a controversial tackle, and AFL Grand Final fallout continues with big TV numbers and trade season ramping up.

stories.title: NRL Grand Final set: Roosters vs Knights at Accor Stadium
stories.why_it_matters: It's Roosters vs Knights in the 2026 NRL Grand Final at Accor Stadium on Sunday 4 October, 6:30pm. The Knights are the surprise package of the finals — Fox Sports notes a $13m player who was considered an 'afterthought' has emerged as a key hero in their run. The Dolphins roster situation is also creating awkward questions around player availability heading into the off-season.

stories.title: Knights' Phoenix Crossland learns fate over sickening Cleary tackle
stories.why_it_matters: Newcastle Knights winger Phoenix Crossland has been sweating on his judiciary result after a controversial tackle on Panthers star Nathan Cleary in the finals. Crossland avoided the 'unwanted company' of players suspended for Grand Final week — his clearance is a significant boost for the Knights heading into Sunday's decider, keeping their best attacking options on the park.

stories.title: AFL Grand Final draws 4.52 million viewers — biggest TV event of 2026
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL Grand Final pulled 4.52 million viewers, making it the biggest TV event in Australia in 2026 so far. That's a massive audience — roughly one in six Australians watched. Fremantle Docker Patrick Voss also went viral after a touching moment of post-match support for his teammates despite the Dockers' loss, which won him widespread praise from AFL fans.

stories.title: AFL trade season: Hawks eyeing deals, Dees hold two top picks
stories.why_it_matters: AFL trade season is kicking off with Hawthorn actively looking to do deals and Melbourne holding two top-10 draft picks — a strong position heading into the draft. The report card across all clubs highlights best and worst moments of 2026 and flags each team's trade priorities. Big moves expected over the next few weeks as clubs reshape their lists.
